title: Gujarat's Swaminarayan
hook: an old teacher calls himself only the drum-beater, and the young yogi from the road gets a new name

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gujarat's Swaminarayan began with Nilkanth, the boy who walked across India with his questions until he reached the ashram at Loj. Did your question go for a walk? Day one thousand four hundred one.

Jay Swaminarayan. In Swaminarayan homes and temples, it's how followers of this tradition say hello, and how they say goodbye, and often how they answer the phone. Two words, run together into one name. But whose name is it? The young yogi who walked into Loj didn't arrive with it. He was Ghanshyam as a child, Nilkanth on the road. Somewhere between that ashram and the greeting on the phone, a name was given, and then a mantra. Today, how the boy from the road became Swaminarayan.
screen: `JAY SWAMINARAYAN` → `A GREETING AND A NAME` → `WHOSE NAME IS IT?`

segments.voice: First, the teacher. Ramanand Swami, whose ashram Nilkanth had reached, was a respected guru in Gujarat with followers of his own. When the two finally met, tradition says Ramanand saw something rare in the young man. He'd once described himself, the story goes, as only the drum-beater, the one who calls the crowd before the real performer arrives. Second, the new name. Ramanand initiated Nilkanth as a sadhu and gave him a new name: Sahajanand Swami, the one whose joy comes naturally. And before long, he chose this newcomer to lead the whole fellowship after him. Third, the mantra. Tradition says that soon after Ramanand died, Sahajanand gave his followers a new name to chant: Swaminarayan. Swami, master. Narayan, a name of God. As people chanted it, they began to call him by it too. And here, the communities that follow him say different things, and say them with care. For some, both words point to him: Sahajanand himself is Swami and Narayan, the Lord. For others, Swami names Gunatitanand Swami, whom they hold as the ideal devotee, and Narayan names Sahajanand, so the one name holds the ideal devotee and God together. They share the mantra, the greeting and the love for him. So this is a name that was given before it was worn, and chanted before it was explained. Now it's a word followers say to each other at the door and on the phone. What do your hellos carry, besides hello?
screen: `RAMANAND, THE DRUM-BEATER` · `NILKANTH BECOMES SAHAJANAND` · `THE MANTRA: SWAMINARAYAN` · `ONE NAME, READ IN DIFFERENT WAYS`

segments.voice: Rest with a name and the breath. Sit, and let the breath find its own pace. Choose one name that matters to you: the name of God in your own tradition, the name of a teacher, or simply a person you're grateful for. Say it inwardly on the in-breath, and rest on the out-breath. When the mind wanders, come back to the name. If you pray in this tradition, you can use the mantra itself, Swaminarayan, as followers do. The bell holds the time.
Gujarat's Swaminarayan. Today, how Nilkanth became Sahajanand Swami under Ramanand, and how the mantra Swaminarayan became his name. Today's word.
Your line: Gujarat's Swaminarayan. Today, put a little more into one greeting: say hello as if it carried a blessing. Day one thousand four hundred one.

howItsDone: Swaminarayan followers greet one another with 'Jay Swaminarayan' and chant the Swaminarayan mantra in daily worship, remembering how Ramanand Swami initiated Nilkanth as Sahajanand Swami.

notes: The greeting Jay Swaminarayan is described without counts; confirm.
Ramanand's 'drum-beater' saying (dugdugi) is given only as 'the story goes'; confirm it is told in the sampradaya.
Sahajanand glossed as 'the one whose joy comes naturally' and Narayan Muni (his other initiation name) left out; confirm the gloss.

The two readings of the name (Sahajanand as both Swami and Narayan; or Gunatitanand as Swami and Sahajanand as Narayan, as BAPS teaches) are stated side by side without ranking. Keepers from each community should check the wording; 'the ideal devotee' is attributed to that reading.
Where the mantra was first given (tradition: Faneni) and dates are omitted under the claims rule.
The original game omits the language label in the note: स्वामिनारायण is the Devanagari form; Gujarati would be સ્વામિનારાયણ. Keeper: choose.
